title: The Battle of the Trench
teaser: Ten thousand men came to finish Madinah. A ditch, a month of cold, and a wind decided it.

layers.title: The Confederacy
layers.subtitle: How ten thousand men came to one town
layers.content:
Arabia had gone quiet for a year. Then twenty chiefs of Banu Nadir, exiled from Madinah and settled at Khaybar, rode to Makkah with an offer. Attack Muhammad ﷺ, and we will stand behind you with everything we have. Quraysh, who had never recovered the reputation they lost at Badr, took it. The same delegation carried the same offer east to Ghatafan, and then to other parts of Arabia. Where they went, they built a coalition.

What gathered outside Madinah in Shawwal of the fifth year had no precedent in the peninsula. Quraysh, Kinanah and allies from Tihamah in the south brought four thousand men under Abu Sufyan. From the east came Banu Sulaym, Ghatafan, Banu Murrah, Fazarah and Ashja' — Fazarah commanded by Uyaynah ibn Hisn, Murrah by al-Harith ibn Awf, Ashja' by Mis'ar ibn Rakhilah. Al-Mubarakpuri puts the assembled force at ten thousand. That number by itself was larger than the entire Muslim population of Madinah, counting the women, the children and the old.

Madinah's scouts tracked the columns and reported them before they arrived, which removed the one advantage a force that size has: surprise. The Prophet ﷺ convened a council and opened the defence of the city to argument. Out of that argument came the proposal of Salman al-Farisi, a Persian who knew how his own people held ground. 'Messenger of Allah, whenever a siege was laid to us in Persia, we would dig trenches to defend ourselves.' No Arab army had ever met that.

Three thousand Muslims took the field. Mountains, boulder fields and dense palm orchards sealed most approaches to the town. Only the north was open. That is where they dug.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Digging
layers.subtitle: Forty yards to every ten men, in hunger
layers.content:
The orders went out at speed. Forty yards of trench were allotted to each working party of ten. The Prophet ﷺ dug with them. Sahl ibn Sa'd said: we were in the company of Allah's Messenger, and some would dig while we carried the dirt out on our backs. The Sealed Nectar records the finished work at roughly five and a half kilometres long, about four and a half metres wide and a little over three metres deep, with the excavated sand heaped on the town side to raise the wall further.

They worked in cold, and they worked hungry. Al-Mubarakpuri describes hunger that came close to starvation, and it did not stop the digging. Jabir ibn Abdullah, seeing that the Prophet ﷺ was starving, slaughtered a lamb and cooked barley and invited him and a few Companions. The Prophet ﷺ called every man on the trench — they were in the thousands. All of them ate until they were full, and the pot and the dough were as they had been. Another day a woman brought a handful of dates. He tossed them in his cloak, called the men, and the dates kept increasing until they spilled from the hem.

One boulder would not break. Al-Bara' said that on the Day of the Trench a huge rock resisted their spades, so they went to Allah's Messenger ﷺ. He took the spade, said 'In the Name of Allah,' and struck. 'Allah is the Most Great. I have been given the keys of Ash-Sham. By Allah, I can see its red palaces at this moment.' He struck again: Persia, and the white palace of Mada'in. The third strike shattered the rest of the rock: the keys of Yemen, and the gates of San'a seen from where he stood. Men digging a ditch out of fear were being told the names of empires.
layers.hadith_ref: The narration of al-Bara' ibn Azib on the boulder at the Trench — reported by an-Nasa'i in as-Sunan al-Kubra and by Ahmad in his Musnad; Ibn Ishaq reports similar from Salman al-Farisi
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: When the Hearts Rose to the Throats
layers.subtitle: A siege, a betrayal behind them, and a wind
layers.content:
The army arrived, camped at al-Asyal and by Uhud, and found the ground cut open in front of it. Cavalry could not cross. So they laid siege and rode the length of the ditch looking for a gap, while the Muslims held Mount Sila' behind it and kept them off with arrows. Amr ibn Abd Wudd, Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl and Dirar ibn al-Khattab forced a crossing and seized a strip of ground between the trench and the mountain. Amr called for a duel. Ali ibn Abi Talib answered and killed him, and the rest withdrew in confusion. The fighting was mostly archery and it cost little: al-Mubarakpuri counts six Muslims and ten of the confederates killed. Sa'd ibn Mu'adh was hit by an arrow that opened an artery in his arm.

The pressure was measured in nights, not casualties. Jabir narrated that Umar came to the Prophet ﷺ cursing the disbelievers of Quraysh and saying he had not prayed Asr and the sun had set. The Prophet ﷺ answered: 'By Allah, I have not prayed it either.' They went to Buthan, made wudu, prayed Asr after sunset, then Maghrib. Other narrations say more prayers than one were delayed. The siege ran over a month.

Then the rear opened. Huyayy ibn Akhtab of Banu Nadir went into the quarter of Banu Qurayzah and worked on their chief, Ka'b ibn Asad, who held a treaty with the Prophet ﷺ obliging him to come to his aid in war. Ka'b refused, then gave way. Qurayzah renounced the treaty and began operations against the outlying parts of the city where the women and children were. Four men — Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, Sa'd ibn Ubadah, Abdullah ibn Rawahah and Khawwat ibn Jubayr — were sent to verify it, and told to keep it quiet if it proved true. It was true.

That is the situation the Qur'an describes: «وَبَلَغَتِ الْقُلُوبُ الْحَنَاجِرَ» — 'and the hearts reached the throats' (33:10-11). An army in front, a broken treaty behind, families in the middle. The believers were tried and shaken with a mighty shaking.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 33:10-11 — 'and the eyes turned aside and the hearts reached the throats... there the believers were tried and shaken with a mighty shaking'
layers.hadith_ref: Jabir ibn Abdullah on the delayed Asr prayer at the Trench — Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: What Surat al-Ahzab Settled
layers.subtitle: The verses that named who stood and who did not
layers.content:
Surat al-Ahzab was revealed around this month, and it does something the sirah alone cannot: it separates the voices inside the city.

Of the hypocrites and the sick-hearted: 'Allah and His Messenger promised us nothing but delusions.' And a party said: 'O people of Yathrib, there is no stand possible for you, so go back.' And a band asked leave of the Prophet ﷺ saying 'our homes lie open' — and they did not lie open; they only wished to flee (33:12-13). Their houses were on the safe side of the town. The excuse is recorded, and so is the fact that it was false.

Of the believers, in the same hour and looking at the same army: 'This is what Allah and His Messenger promised us, and Allah and His Messenger spoke the truth' — and it added nothing to them but faith and submission (33:22). Two readings of one horizon.

On the ending, the Qur'an gives no human author. «فَأَرْسَلْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ رِيحًا وَجُنُودًا لَّمْ تَرَوْهَا» — 'so We sent against them a wind, and forces you did not see' (33:9). And: «وَكَفَى اللَّهُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ الْقِتَالَ» — 'and Allah sufficed the believers against fighting' (33:25). The confederates went home having gained no good.

The surah then turns to those who had backed them from behind the walls, and to what followed (33:26-27). It also carries the ruling that the Prophet ﷺ is not the father of any of the men, but the Messenger of Allah and the seal of the prophets — a separate matter of that year, settled in the same revelation.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 33:9 — 'so We sent against them a wind, and forces you did not see'; Quran 33:12-13, 33:22, 33:25
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: How It Broke, and What Followed
layers.subtitle: An arbitration, a death, a reversed direction
layers.content:
Before the wind, the alliance had already been split from inside. Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud of Ghatafan told the Prophet ﷺ he had accepted Islam in secret and asked to be used; he was told to do whatever he judged useful. He advised Qurayzah not to fight beside Quraysh without holding hostages as security, told Quraysh that Qurayzah regretted the break and would hand any hostages to the Muslims, and said the same to his own tribe. When messages passed that Saturday night, each side read the other exactly as Nu'aym had taught it to. Then wind, rain and hard cold tore out their tents and overturned their cooking pots. Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, sent out that night, found them packing to leave.

The Prophet ﷺ moved on Banu Qurayzah the day he returned, the banner with Ali. The forts held out twenty-five days. Abu Lubabah, sent in at their request, signalled to his throat that death awaited them, then tied himself to a pillar of the mosque until Allah forgave him. When the tribe surrendered to the Prophet's judgement, al-Aws interceded for their old allies, so he offered arbitration by Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, their former confederate. Both sides accepted, and Sa'd was told his verdict would bind everyone present. He ruled that the fighting men be put to death, the women and children taken captive, the property divided. The Prophet ﷺ accepted it, saying Sa'd had judged by the command of Allah. Huyayy ibn Akhtab, who had engineered the break, was executed. One woman was put to death, for killing a Muslim with a grinding stone.

Then Sa'd's own wound opened and he died of it. Jabir narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said the Throne of the Most Merciful shook at the death of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh.

Of the siege the Prophet ﷺ said afterwards: 'From now we engage them, and they will not engage us.' Carry this: almost nobody died at the Trench. A month of digging, cold, hunger and rumour is what the Qur'an calls a mighty shaking. Endurance with no battle to show for it is still the thing being measured.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 33:25 — 'and Allah sufficed the believers against fighting'
layers.hadith_ref: 'The Throne of the Most Merciful shook at the death of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh' — narrated by Jabir, Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

quiz.prompt: Whose proposal was it to defend Madinah by digging a trench?

options.text: Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, chief of al-Aws
Salman al-Farisi, who had seen sieges in Persia
Abu Bakr as-Siddiq
Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman

quiz.scholar_reflection: The Prophet ﷺ opened the defence of the city to discussion and took the plan of a Persian freedman. Nothing like it had been used in Arabia before.

quiz.prompt: What were the two armies at the Trench, as al-Mubarakpuri gives them?

options.text: About 3,000 Muslims against about 10,000 confederates
313 Muslims against 1,000 Quraysh
700 Muslims against 3,000 confederates
1,000 Muslims against 4,000 Quraysh

quiz.scholar_reflection: Quraysh, Kinanah and Tihamah brought four thousand under Abu Sufyan; Ghatafan, Sulaym, Murrah, Fazarah and Ashja' made up the rest. The total outnumbered every soul in Madinah.

quiz.prompt: Who split the confederacy from inside by making each ally distrust the others?

options.text: Abdullah ibn Rawahah
Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud of Ghatafan, who had accepted Islam in secret
Uyaynah ibn Hisn of Fazarah
Khawwat ibn Jubayr

quiz.scholar_reflection: He asked to be used, was told to do whatever he judged useful, and went three times: to Qurayzah, to Quraysh, to his own tribe. The messages that passed that Saturday night were read exactly as he had taught them to be read.

quiz.prompt: How did the siege of Madinah actually end?

options.text: A pitched battle in which the confederates were routed
The Muslims paid Ghatafan a third of Madinah's fruit crop to withdraw
Distrust among the allies, then wind, rain and hard cold that wrecked their camp
Quraysh accepted a treaty on the spot

quiz.citation: Quran 33:9 and 33:25 — Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: The offer of a third of the fruit crop was raised and then dropped after the two Sa'ds objected. In the end the Qur'an names the cause: a wind, and forces you did not see.

quiz.prompt: Who delivered the ruling on Banu Qurayzah after their surrender?

options.text: The Prophet ﷺ ruled on them directly
Ali ibn Abi Talib, who held the banner
Abu Lubabah, whom they had asked for
Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, arbitrating with both sides' agreement

quiz.scholar_reflection: Al-Aws interceded for their old allies, so the Prophet ﷺ offered arbitration by Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, Qurayzah's former confederate. Sa'd asked whether his verdict would bind everyone present, including the Prophet ﷺ, and was told it would.

quiz.prompt: Six men died on the Muslim side across more than a month. The Qur'an still calls it a mighty shaking. What does that tell you about what a trial actually is?

options.text: The waiting and the cold were harder than fighting would have been
The real weight was the betrayal behind them, not the army in front
Trials are measured by what they do to the heart, not by the body count
A test with nothing dramatic to show for it is the hardest kind to hold

quiz.slider_label: How much of what has tested you most had nothing visible to show?
quiz.scholar_reflection: There was no Badr here. There was digging, hunger, arrows over a ditch, and a rumour that the rear was open. That is what was called a shaking.

quiz.prompt: Men digging a defensive ditch out of fear were told they would be given the keys of Sham, Persia and Yemen. What is that doing at that moment?

options.text: Enlarging the horizon of people whose horizon had shrunk to one ditch
Testing whether they would believe a promise that contradicted what they could see
Reframing the labour: they were not surviving, they were beginning
Giving them something to remember later, once it came true

quiz.slider_label: When your situation narrows, how far ahead can you still see?
quiz.citation: The narration of al-Bara' on the boulder — reported by an-Nasa'i and Ahmad; Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: The hypocrites mocked exactly this — talk of Kisra and Caesar from men pinned behind a ditch. Both groups heard the same words.

quiz.prompt: The Qur'an records the excuse of those who left the trench — 'our homes lie open' — and then records that it was not true. Why preserve a false excuse in scripture?

options.text: So the pattern can be recognised later, in other people and in oneself
Because the excuse was reasonable-sounding, which is what made it dangerous
To show that Allah judges the motive, not the wording
To make plain that withdrawal was a choice, not a necessity

quiz.slider_label: How often do your reasons for stepping back describe a real constraint?
quiz.citation: Quran 33:13 — 'And they lay not open. They but wished to flee'
quiz.scholar_reflection: Their houses were on the protected side of the town. The verse does not argue with them; it simply states the fact and moves on.

quiz.prompt: Banu Qurayzah held a treaty obliging them to come to Madinah's aid in war, and instead moved against the city's undefended quarters while the siege was on. Sitting with only what the sources record, what weighs most for you?

options.text: That the treaty was a mutual defence pact, broken at the worst possible hour
That Ka'b ibn Asad refused Huyayy at first and was worked on until he gave way
That the judgement was an arbitration both parties agreed to accept in advance
That it is a hard episode and should be read slowly, not used as a slogan

quiz.slider_label: How comfortable are you leaving a hard account unsimplified?
quiz.scholar_reflection: The sources give a sequence: a standing treaty, a repudiation during a siege, a surrender, an intercession by al-Aws, an agreed arbitrator, a verdict. Holding all six in view is harder and more honest than holding one.

quiz.prompt: After the confederates left, the Prophet ﷺ said: 'From now we engage them, and they will not engage us.' What kind of change is that?

options.text: Military — Madinah stops defending and starts choosing where things happen
Psychological — the largest force Arabia could raise had failed, and everyone knew it
Political — the watching tribes now had a different answer to who would last
Personal — a community that had been reacting for years stopped reacting

quiz.slider_label: Where in your life are you still reacting rather than choosing?
quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari — the Prophet's words after the withdrawal of the Confederates
quiz.scholar_reflection: Nothing in the balance of numbers had changed. What changed was that a coalition of ten thousand had come, spent a month, and gone home with nothing.
